title: SLO Evidence Taxonomy and Capacity Orchestrator SDK Runbook
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary:
This document defines a company-standard taxonomy for SLO evidence, retention rules, and automated packaging used for incident reviews and capacity orchestration. It also provides a runbook for the Capacity Orchestrator SDK (internal tooling) that ties SLO signals to safe, auditable capacity actions and error budget governance. The goal is repeatable, forensically-sound evidence capture + automated, reversible capacity changes when error budgets are consumed.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: All customer-facing model serving and API endpoints managed by Redwood inference clusters (hosted, dedicated, private control plane).
- Audience: Oncall SREs, reliability engineers, incident responders, runbook authors, and platform automation engineers.

Why this exists:
- Reduce friction between incident evidence collection and postmortem quality by standardizing what is captured and how long it is kept.
- Ensure capacity actions (scale-up, throttles, preemptions) are traceable, reversible, and tied to SLO ownership and error budget policies.

Key definitions (terminology):
- Evidence Snapshot: Atomic capture containing telemetry, traces, sample payloads, and configuration snapshot relevant to an SLO incident window.
- SLO Signal: Metric used to evaluate an SLO (e.g., p99 latency, success rate).
- Error Budget Burn Rate: Multiplier of expected error budget consumption per hour.
- Capacity Orchestrator: Internal SDK and control-plane integration that applies capacity changes (reservations, preemption, traffic shaping) with audit metadata.

Evidence Taxonomy (what to capture for every SLO alert):
1) Telemetry baseline (required)
   - Time series segment: metric vector for the incident window +/- 10m.
   - Aggregates: 5m/1m/30s rollups for p50/p95/p99/p99.9 where applicable.
2) Traces (high-priority)
   - Full traces for sampled requests hitting the failing path (min 100 traces, or 1000 if sample rate > 1%). Include service spans: router -> inference runtime -> gpu-scheduler -> cache layer.
3) Representative request payloads (anonymized)
   - Up to 200 requests (strip PII) that triggered the SLO violation.
4) Model & runtime config snapshot
   - model version, quantization profile, batch config, kernel selection, GPU assignment, and autoscale settings.
5) Routing/traffic policy snapshot
   - active routing rules, canaries, fallback policies, and tenant fair-share quotas in effect.
6) Capacity & host state
   - host-level CPU/GPU metrics, oom logs, driver restarts, and node labels.
7) Alert rule + evaluation context
   - full query and evaluation window for the alert that fired.
8) Audit metadata (required)
   - who ran the snapshot (user/tool), timestamp, runbook version, and any capacity actions applied.

Retention matrix (minimums):
- Critical SLO incidents (severity P0/P1): Evidence snapshots retained 365 days.
- Moderate incidents (P2): 90 days retention.
- Routine evidence (daily SLO checks, no violation): 30 days.
- Derived artifacts (aggregated reports, runbook notes): 540 days.

Retention table (described):
- Column: Incident severity | Retention TTL | Owner for deletion approval
- Row: P0/P1 | 365d | Service Stewards + Legal hold feature
- Row: P2 | 90d | Service Stewards
- Row: Info | 30d | SRE Observability team

Evidence capture workflow (step-by-step):
1) Alert triggers SLO policy -> Pager routed to oncall.
2) Pager action invokes observability-hook that:
   a) Creates an Evidence Snapshot job (Observability API v2).
   b) Tags snapshot with slo_id, service, incident_id, and owner_team.
3) Snapshot producer runs collectors in parallel: timeseries, traces, payload-sampler, node-state polls, and config-dump.
4) Snapshot upload to internal evidence-bucket with encryption and retention TTL, returning snapshot_id.
5) If error budget burn > 2x sustained for 30m (configurable threshold), Capacity Orchestrator SDK receives a signed action request (see Capacity triggers).

Automated evidence sampling rules (to reduce cost):
- Sampling tiers:
  - Tier A (critical paths): deterministic sampling for all requests for 10m after trigger.
  - Tier B (high-volume non-critical tenants): reservoir sampling capped at 200 requests.
  - Tier C (background health checks): summary-only (no payloads).
- PII scrubbing rules: remove fields named: email, ssn, token, password, account_id; mask any field matching regex ("\\d{12,}").

Capacity Orchestrator: triggers and safe actions
SLOs and thresholds (examples):
- inference-success-rate (SLO: 99.95% over 7d, error budget 0.05%)
- api-p99-latency (SLO: < 350ms p99 over 30d)
- streaming-tail-p99_9 (SLO: < 2s p99.9 over 30d)

Trigger matrix (automated):
- Trigger A: sustained error budget burn > 3x for 60 minutes -> mark for human review + create capacity action draft (no autoplace).
- Trigger B: sustained error budget burn > 8x for 20 minutes AND host signals (GPU OOMs) -> autoplace scaled reserve nodes (see actions).
- Trigger C: systemic p99 degradation with tenant impact score > 0.5 -> traffic shaping rollout to degrade non-core tenants first.

Allowed capacity actions (examples and audit fields):
- reserve_capacity: request additional reserved GPU nodes (min 1, max 20)
  - required audit fields: snapshot_id, trigger_id, requested_by (service account), reason, rollback_window_minutes
- preempt_noncritical_pools: drain and preempt pools tagged noncritical=true
  - required audit fields: snapshot_id, preempt_list, time_box_minutes
- emergency_throttle: apply token-rate limits at ingress per-tenant percentage
  - required audit fields: snapshot_id, throttle_policy_id, expected_cost_savings

Capacity Orchestrator SDK examples (pseudo-CLI and YAML):
- CLI (human-mediated draft):
  rcoctl draft-action --service inference-prod --trigger-id TRG-12345 --action reserve_capacity --nodes 4 --rollback 60 --reason "p99 latency x8 burn"

- SDK call (Python):
  from rco.sdk import OrchestratorClient
  client = OrchestratorClient(auth_token=os.getenv('RCO_TOKEN'))
  res = client.create_action(service='inference-prod', trigger_id='TRG-12345', action='reserve_capacity', spec={'nodes':4}, snapshot_id='SNAP-20260902-001', enforced_by='auto')
  print(res.action_id)

Audit & approval model:
- All automated actions must create an action record with status = [draft | pending_approval | applied | rolled_back].
- Human approval required for actions that request > 8 nodes or that have rollback_window_minutes > 240.
- Approvals are recorded in the evidence snapshot and linked in postmortem artifacts.

Runbook: Immediate steps for oncall (condensed):
1) Confirm the alert & ownership: verify sla_owner and service_steward in service registry.
2) Launch Evidence Snapshot (if not already started): run `observctl snapshot create --incident $INCIDENT_ID` and confirm snapshot_id.
3) Run health checks (use scripts below). Collect results in a structured note.
4) Evaluate burn rate using the mini-calc script: see appendix.
5) If burn rate > 8x AND node OOMs or driver restarts exist -> follow Automated capacity action path (autoplace) OR if autoplace disabled, trigger the draft via rcoctl and call for approval.
6) If burn rate between 3x-8x, escalate to oncall lead and create mitigation plan, consider temporary throttles or canary rollback.
7) After stabilization, mark runbook steps as evidence and set retention appropriately.

Emergency mitigation checklist (quick):
- Toggle safe-mode routing: enable fallback variants (runtime config toggle: fallbacks.enabled=true).
- Activate per-tenant throttles at 10% increments (max 50%) starting from lowest-priority tenants.
- Increase sampling reduction for traces to save evidence budget (observctl sampling set --rate 0.1).

Verification and validation steps (post-action):
- Verify service-level telemetry returns below threshold within rollback_window_minutes/2.
- Confirm snapshot_id is attached to the action and stored.
- Run smoke tests: config-check, end-to-end request against canary model, and a deterministic latency probe (curl sample + timing).

Post-incident packaging for incident review (deliverables):
- Incident writeup (markdown) with links to snapshot_id, action_id, and timelines.
- Evidence bundle: timeseries.csv, traces.zip, config.yaml, sample-requests.json (PII-scrubbed).
- Change record: any capacity or config change applied, with commit id and rollout window.

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Oncall SRE: run immediate runbook, capture snapshots, and request capacity actions when necessary.
- Service steward: make policy decisions for tenant impact and retention exception requests.
- Observability team: ensure snapshot pipeline health and retention enforcement.
- Platform automation: maintain the Capacity Orchestrator SDK and approval workflows.

Template checklists (to copy into incident):
- [ ] Evidence snapshot created and snapshot_id recorded.
- [ ] Top 100 traces archived.
- [ ] Config dump captured.
- [ ] Capacity action drafted (if required).
- [ ] Human approvals collected (if required).
- [ ] Post-incident artifacts packaged and linked.

Appendix A — Useful commands and example queries:
- create evidence snapshot (CLI):
  observctl snapshot create --service inference-prod --window "-10m:+10m" --include traces,payloads,config --tag incident:$INCIDENT_ID

- quick burn rate calc (SQL-like pseudo):
  SELECT service, SUM(errors) / SUM(requests) as error_rate, (error_rate / SLO_target) as burn_rate FROM telemetry.requests WHERE timestamp >= now() - interval '1h' GROUP BY service;

- example PromQL alert fragment for sustained burn:
  (increase(service_errors_total[30m]) / increase(service_requests_total[30m])) / (1 - 0.9995) > 3

Appendix B — Health check script snippets (bash):
- latency probe:
  for i in 1 2 3; do time curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TEST_TOKEN" -d '{"prompt":"hello"}' https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate; done

- node-state gatherer (kubectl example):
  kubectl get pods -l app=inference -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}'
